  "headline": "The Deadly Price of Slowing Down AI",
  "subtitle": "Caution has a body count. It just isn't printed on the label.",
  "body_markdown": "Here's a number that never makes it onto the protest signs: 200 million.

That's how many protein structures — the molecular shapes that decide whether a drug can grab a virus or a tumor — one AI system predicted and posted free for every biologist on Earth. Before it, mapping a single structure could eat a doctoral thesis. Researchers called it decades of biology arriving at once. Notice that nobody demanded a pause first.

I hold a conviction that gets me shouted at dinner parties: the biggest danger in artificial intelligence is not that we build too fast. It's that we govern it into a coma. Every proposal to pause, license and pre-approve treats delay as free. Delay has a price list, and the people on it never get invited to the hearings. We should be deploying these systems at full speed — with seatbelts, not roadblocks.

Start with the price list. Bringing a single drug to market takes a decade or more and, by the industry's own accounting, over $2 billion — and nine in ten candidates that enter human trials fail. AI is already attacking every stage of that pipeline; molecules designed by models are in human trials right now. One was designed in months for a lung disease that had resisted researchers for decades. Run the arithmetic. If these tools cut even two years off the average drug's crawl to patients, then every year spent "deliberating" whether to allow them erases two years of cures the dying will not get back.

And it gets worse. Roughly 7,000 rare diseases afflict some 300 million people, and about 95 percent have no approved treatment at all. For them, the status quo isn't caution. It's a death sentence with paperwork attached.

The deeper pattern is older than silicon. Within 50 years of Gutenberg's press, Europe printed more books than scribes had produced in the previous thousand. Electricity took two generations to reach half of American homes — the lag was wires, not committees. Linux, built by strangers shipping code without anyone's permission, now runs most of the internet, including the servers hosting the arguments for central control. Every large leap in human welfare came from millions of decentralized experiments. The printing press wasn't licensed. It was answered — by literacy, criticism and more books.

Now ask who benefits when you install a gate. An approval regime that costs tens of millions in compliance doesn't stop the technology; the most capable open models have already been downloaded
